meta.title: Accelerating Integer-Quantized AI and Related Workloads in a Space-Grade Multicore Processor via SWAR ISA Extensions

abstract: This paper describes how SIMD Within A Register (SWAR) custom instruction set architecture extensions have been added to the GR765 multicore RISC-V/SPARC space-grade processor. These extensions help speed up low-precision quantized arithmetic operations, which are common in AI workloads. The work also covers changes made to the software stack, compiler, and debugging support that allow SWAR to be used. Benchmark results show a performance boost for typical space-related applications, including those based on machine learning, when SWAR is activated. Additionally, for the AI components, we present a space-qualified inference engine that has a modular mathematical backend that relies on the concept of micro-kernels to implement deep neural network operators for a RISC-V core (NOEL-V) and SWAR, showing the speedup achieved on the OBPMark-ML performance framework when SWAR is enabled.

blocks.html: The European Space Agency (ESA) has developed five generations of LEON processors based on the SPARC open instruction set architecture (ISA), supporting over twenty thousand missions. The open ISA facilitates licensing, customization, and adaptation to space requirements. However, SPARC is becoming outdated, and its user base is decreasing. NASA and ESA are now investing in RISC- V processor chips as a successor [1], with several ESAfunded projects underway. Among these developments is the GR765, a radiation-hardened, fault-tolerant octa-core system-on-chip (SoC) [2], manufactured on a 28nm FDSOI process, which will soon be taped out in 2026, making it one of the first space processors to incorporate RISC-V cores. The GR765 includes both SPARC and RISC-V ISA, giving the user the choice, via a bootstrap signal, between LEON5-FT (SPARC V8) or NOEL-V (RV64) RISC-V processor cores, complemented by high-speed interfaces such as SpaceFibre, PCIe Gen3, SpaceWire, and Ethernet.

Space processor development is costly due to strict environmental and functional requirements. Chips must tolerate radiation, extreme temperatures, vacuum, and vibration while providing specialized capabilities such as interfaces, fault detection, and deterministic execution. Because production volumes are low, development often depends on public funding. Consequently, processors must remain versatile enough to support a variety of workloads, from space-specific tasks to emerging applications such as artificial intelligence (AI). Open instruction set architectures such as RISC-V help address this need by enabling custom instructions to optimize specific functions.

The SWAR (SIMD withing a register) extensions, were proposed for LEON2-FT [3], to improve the execution of GNSS tracking loop, then adapted and integrated in the NOEL-V RISC-V core, [4] and later adopted in the GR765 architecture for both LEON5-FT and NOEL-V. SWAR can accelerate applications that perform many fixed-point operations on quantized data, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), central to AI workloads. Custom processor extensions require hardware development and software stack updates (compiler, simulator, debugging tools). While RISC-V facilitates customization through modularity, careful architectural design and verification are still required to ensure reliability.

This work presents the integration of SWAR extensions into the GR765 processor architecture and the corresponding modifications to the software stack. Performance benefits are demonstrated through speedups on multiple benchmarks, including AI workloads. We also report results from an ESA-funded initiative to port an existing AI inference engine leveraging a lightweight, lock-free data-pipelining framework optimized for high-performance edge computing to the NOEL-V architecture with SWAR integration. The project included alignment with ECSS-E-40 and ECSS- Q-80 space engineering standards for AI under RTEMS and Linux, ensuring high-throughput SWAR capabilities in a mission-qualified software environment.

blocks.html: SWAR can increase processor performance for tasks such as software defined radio (SDR) processing, e.g. for Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), audio and video processing and generic low precision integer arithmetic. The current implementation groups SWAR operations by application domains in one or more arithmetic logic units (ALUs), each constituting a SWAR module, connected in parallel to the main processor ALU.

At the machine level, SWAR operations execute in a single cycle. Two distinct instruction opcodes, swar and swarcc, trigger execution with or without flag updates. Existing instructions such as wrasr/rdasr or csrwr/csrrd configure execution parameters (e.g., enabling/disabling reduction, signed/unsigned saturation) and optionally read accumulated results. Source operands are passed through registers rs1,rs2 or as immediate values (instead of rs2). Results are available in one clock cycle in the destination register rd, while accumulated results can be accessed in high precision via the rdasr or csrrd instruction.

At the hardware level, all SWAR modules share a common input/output interface. Data is exchanged through the processor’s existing full-width data buses (32- or 64bit). Up to thirty-two internal accumulators, each up to 128 bits, connect to the output interface. Adjusted or saturated results are returned within one clock cycle, while precise results require additional instructions—one per 32 (or 64) bits—meaning two instructions are needed to read a full 64-bit (128-bit) accumulator.

Figure 1 shows a block diagram of a general-purpose SWAR ALU that supports additions, subtractions, multiplications and right-shift operations in independent data lanes. SWAR enables efficient implementation of complex mapreduce patterns for computations based on low-precision values, as shown in Figure 2.

blocks.title: SWAR integration with RISC-V/SPARC multicore space processor

blocks.html: SWAR is enabled for both LEON5FT and NOEL-V in the GR765 implementation. It was observed in initial trials that enabling all SWAR modules reduced the maximum processor core frequency, so SWAR was ultimately implemented with only 8- and 16-bit operation support, resulting in die area increase for the processor pipeline of less than 10%.

Four main extensions were implemented for SWAR. First, RISC-V–compliant control was added over the visibility of and access to SWAR control and accumulation registers, allowing software to determine whether accumulators have been used and need saving/restoring during context switches. Second, interlocks were introduced to eliminate the need for NOP padding between configuration register accesses and SWAR operations, or before reading accumulated results. Third, registers were added to enable software to identify SWAR availability and capabilities. Finally, the capabilities of the SWAR operations themselves were extended.

The SWAR use of opcodes is restricted by the SPARC V8 heritage. In the RISC-V case, the situation is different, and it is possible to make use of additional opcodes to encode information that would otherwise require a write to the SWAR configuration register. SWAR uses the major opcode, CUSTOM1, where it leaves 10 bits (7 bits needed for CUSTOM1, 3x5 for rd/rs1/rs2) unused. An update was made to NOEL-V/SWAR that made it possible to encode the 8/16 bit ALU operations directly. The SWAR configuration register is thus no longer needed. The original SWAR opcode remains and can be used, as it is required for other SWAR functionality should it be added back in.

The new encoding has been simplified. Two bits select among the four main ALU operations (add, subtract, multiply, shift right), one bit selects between 8- and 16-bit ALU operations, and one bit determines whether an unsigned × signed multiplication yields a signed result. Another bit selects variations of the ALU operations, such as averaging or rounded multiplication. Additional bits control reduction, saturation, normalization, and signedness, with certain previously unused combinations repurposed to provide new functionality, such as widening results or accessing high and low halves.

To further improve the utility of SWAR, several custom extensions were added to the normal ALUs, utilizing the CUSTOM0 and CUSTOM2 opcodes. These include combining two words (after optional rotation) using a mask, quickly creating masks in various ways, and rapidly generating permutation constants for XPERM8 through multiple methods.

As a test, a hand optimized 8-bit 5x5 convolution filter was implemented in assembly language using SWAR (and one extra NOEL-V ALU instruction for data movement). This was compared to a well optimized version in C, with both running completely from L1 caches.

The assembly code made use of SWAR to multiply the five filter coefficients of one row by the corresponding signal data, and sum up the results, in a single instruction. Both implementations take 80 clock cycles to execute. The achievable speedup is limited by the summing of the five row results, data movement and various housekeeping, but there is still an 8x improvement (see Table 1).

blocks.title: Using SWAR in the software stack

blocks.html: A compiler-driven approach is employed to integrate SWAR. By extending the LLVM[5] RISC-V backend with support for the standard LLVM v8i8 and v4i16 data types, tying those to the corresponding SWAR instructions, the general vectorization machinery of LLVM can be employed, with Clang and other LLVM frontends. Two custom processor profiles were created for NOEL-V to make the SWAR support explicitlyoptional.

Significant performance benefits were realized even in this non-SWAR profile, by using more instruction set extensions, as well as improving scheduling and instruction alignment. Due to the in-order nature of NOEL-V, proper instruction scheduling at the compiler stage becomes highly crucial.

In addition, vector manipulation was tuned to use bitmanipulation extensions, including the XPERM8 instruction, and the new proprietary RORMIXI instruction for fixed-pattern masking operations. Memory coalescing was implemented so that e.g. 8 8-bit loads or 2 32-bit loads are realized using a single 64-bit load, rather than multiple narrow loads, when this was probably safe. NOEL-V can issue two general instructions per cycle, but at most one memory access, making this transformation beneficial. It is thus faster to unpack a loaded 64-bit word using the ALU rather than doing multiple loads. Without this change, we experienced scenarios where the SWAR support was fast, but data accesses were scalarized.

The IREE project was used to transform quantized AI models into MLIR[6] form, then using LLVM to compile them for bare-metal execution. IREE was mildly modified to explicitly use SWAR scalar products for convolutions, and to better tag alignment information in the resulting LLVM IR. This was modeled on a similar transformation pass for the ARM Neon architecture in the related case of matrix-matrix-transpose multiplications.

In parallel, an ESA-funded project ported an existing lock-free, modular AI inference framework to the NOEL-V architecture. While the original used standard RV64GC micro-kernels, a specialized micro-kernel was implemented to exploit NOEL-V’s SWAR extensions (Figure 3). Inner loops were reorganized to process eight 8-bit multiplyaccumulate operations simultaneously using SWAR intrinsics in multiply-reduction mode, producing a single partial sum from two packed 64-bit operands. The same mechanism was also used to accelerate zero-point compensation during requantization.

The performance of the SWAR operations has been first assessed on computation of simple FIR filters. Both off-line and on-line filters were considered, with processing buffers organized linearly, or as circular buffers, or as aligned circular buffers. Figure 4 shows the number of instructions for one iteration of online FIR filters with up to 50 taps, computed with and without the SWAR instructions and using buffers organized in three different ways.

blocks.html: The modified compiler stack described in Section 4 was used to execute parts of space oriented software benchmarks, OBPMark (image processing and AES encryption) and OBPMark-ML (cloud detection by semantic segmentation)[7]. The pre-trained network for the semantic segmentation task is a small U-Net-like convolutional design. A pre-quantized version in tflite format was available. This could be processed completely unchanged in IREE.

For OBPMark, we added general annotation to the C++ code to aid the compiler, such as buffer alignment and using the restrict and const keywords to assert the lack of pointer aliasing and non-changing. We also changed loop orders to improve memory locality. For the image processing test, 800 128x128 frames were used. For AES the length of the plaintext was 16M bytes, with 128-bit keys, Nb 4, Nk 4, Nr 10.

We compare the results with a NOEL-V LLVM profile including SWAR, NOEL-V without SWAR, and plain LLVM (for target rv64imafdc) in Table 2. We also compare to the Gaisler gcc-based NCC compiler distribution for those tests that did not rely on the IREE stack. Even the plain LLVM had some of our memory coalescing optimizations. These experiments were executed in an FPGA environment clocked at 75MHz with a preliminary version of the SWAR implementation where the pipeline was held for 2 cycles for each SWAR instruction. Later prototypes have a fully pipelined SWAR handling (2-cycle latency) and co-schedule SWAR and memory operations.

In the image processing benchmark, execution time decreased by over 40% compared to plain LLVM and slightly less relative to NCC, as some 32-bit steps cannot benefit from SWAR. AES achieved nearly 60% reduction versus LLVM and even more relative to NCC. Semantic segmentation, dominated by tight 8-bit convolutions, saw almost 75% reduction.

blocks.html: In a convolution kernel, a single reducing SWAR scalar product can replace 15 scalar instructions. Although the NOEL-V prototype can execute up to four scalar ALU instructions in two cycles but only one SWAR instruction, the nearly 75% time reduction remains impressive. Memory accesses, register spilling, and non-convolutional netowork layers (pooling and re-quantization)—the latter requiring 32-bit scalar math—also affect the results.

The optimized inference engine described in Section 4.1was evaluated using the OBPMark-ML framework with two space-based workloads: Ship Detection and Lunanet, both using uint8 quantization. Benchmark results confirm that the integration of NOEL-V SWAR extensions significantly accelerates data processing. The parallel SWAR-optimized micro-kernels achieved a 3x reduction in latency compared to the scalar baseline, as seen in Table 3.

We have shown how adding SWAR custom instructions to a RISC-V processor core can boost execution of several applications where low bit rate arithmetic operations are executed, such as AI workloads. Results are demonstrated in its integration in a multicore development for space, the GR765 exhibiting execution time reductions of up to 75% at a very low die are increase for the processor pipeline of less than 10%. Details are providing on the efforts that need to be made in the software stack to benefit from SWAR, and a AI software framework that leverages SWAR was also presented.
